chapter_theme: The invocation to Shiva and Akananuru 1 to 20 in the anthology's fixed order of lands: paalai poems of men leaving or turning back for wealth and of mothers whose daughters eloped, Kapilar's hill courtships in which the friend presses for marriage, mullai homecomings at evening, neythal shores closed by gossip, and marutham quarrels over the husband's women. Chola, Chera, Pandya and lesser chiefs' names (Thithan's Uranthai, Thondi, Kodai, Avi's Pothini, Nannan's Pazhi) serve as measures of private beauty, guard and loss.

0.reading: The god wears fresh konrai blossom as garland and chaplet, a fine thread on his chest, an unwinking eye on his brow, axe and pick in hand and a three-pointed spear; he rides the bull with Umai beside him, red as the evening sky, with crescent-white teeth, flame-bright matted hair lit by the young moon, a tiger's hide and a dark throat, and the world rests in the shade of his flawless feet, an old order no god or sage has fathomed.
0.nuance: The poem is a list of possessions in short clauses (மார்பினஃதே, நுதலது, கையது, ஊர்ந்தது, சேர்ந்தோள்) and gives its only verb of the world at the end: the whole world has stopped (தவிர்ந்தன்று) in the shade of his feet. Unlike the Purananuru's opening by a poet of the same name, it sets Umai beside him rather than inside him, a fitting choice for an anthology of love.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god, கடவுள் வாழ்த்து (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the konrai blossom, gold-coloured
the god's body, red as the evening sky
his white curved teeth, like the bright crescent
his bright twisted matted hair, like rising flame

1.reading: The woman asks her friend whether he has forgotten his word that they would never part, a bond he likened to stone set with lac at Avi's Pothini, now that he has left, her shoulders slackening, to fetch gold from a far country across a forest where the sun has stripped the trees of shade, dried the springs, parches spilt grain, emptied the road even of robbers, and where wind-tossed murungai blossom looks like sea spray.
1.nuance: She does not accuse; she asks whether he forgot (மறந்தனர் கொல்லோ), which keeps the fault in memory rather than in will. The promise was itself a simile of permanence, stone fixed with lac, set against a land where everything is coming loose: shade, water, people. Line 5 recurs verbatim in Akananuru 356.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman speaks of a man gone across the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: Avi, a war-leader like Murugan
the lovers' promised bond, like stone set fast with lac
her shoulders, like bamboo
the sun's rays, burning like fire
the white murungai blossom blown up by the wind, like the spray of breaking waves
the blossom-swept forest, looking like the sea

2.reading: The friend tells the hill lord that on his slopes a male monkey drinks without knowing it the wine that ripe jackfruit and plantain have made in a rock pool, cannot climb the pepper-twined sandal tree and sleeps content on the flowered slope; if beasts there find unplanned joy so easily, how can the joy he plans be hard for him, when the girl's heart cannot be held back and he may yet come at night, slipping past her father's watchmen, though the vengai has burst into flower and the full moon has risen.
2.nuance: The friend states the moral of the monkey herself (குறியா இன்பம் ... குறித்த இன்பம்), so this is an open comparison, not ullurai; a traditional further reading makes the drunk monkey that cannot climb the lover who will not rise to marriage. The closing signs are a warning dressed as permission: the vengai's flowering is the season of the girl's confinement and the moon lights the path he would take by night.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறிக்கட் செறிப்பறிவுறீஇத் தோழி வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: secret meeting under the father's watch, on the hill slopes

comparisons.tenor: the monkey's unplanned joy set beside the joy the hero plans and delays
the girl's shoulders, like bamboo

3.reading: The man tells his heart, which showed him the long road through the waste and pushed him from behind toward wealth, that its lie, which looks like truth, cannot lift his grief when on that far road the glance of the girl with the red mouth and sweet speech, eyes that rival her curved earrings, comes across his way; and the road is the one where a red-eared vulture, to feed its mate weak from laying in the omai tree, ceaselessly tears like looters at the rotting wild cow a tiger killed and left.
3.nuance: The heart stands behind and drives (பின்நின்று துரக்கும்), the very phrase another paalai poet uses for a heart that stays behind and holds back (Akananuru 19). The vulture that forages for a nesting mate is the man's own errand seen from the road, and its carrion feast makes the wealth he is promised look like plunder.

colophon.thurai: முன்னொரு காலத்து நெஞ்சினாற் பொருள்வலிக்கப்பட்டுப் பிரிந்தான் தலைமகன்; பிரிந்து இடைச்சுரத்தினின்று அவள் நலநயந்து மீளலுற்ற நெஞ்சினைக் கழறிப்போய்ப் பொருண் முடித்துவந்தவன் பின்னும் பொருள்வலிக்கப்பட்ட நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லிச் செலவழுங்கியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a man argues with the heart that drives him across the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the dark rough bark of the omai, like a crocodile's back
the vulture tearing at carrion, like plunderers
the heart's promise, a lie that looks like truth
her red mouth, like the coral-tree petal

iraicchi.act: the male vulture flies out hungry to bring food to its mate, who has laid and lies weak in the nest
iraicchi.sense: a male's errand is for the mate he leaves weak at home, which is the very claim of the heart's errand for wealth and the reason the man turns back to her

4.reading: The friend shows the woman the season: jasmine has put out its tips, konrai buds open, the stag with horns like twisted iron leaps into the gravel hollows and rain has made the forest lovely; look, there comes the chariot of the lord of the low hills, its reins drawn taut as lute-strings and its bell-tongues tied so as not to startle the nectar birds asleep with their mates in the flowering boughs, as he comes thinking of her beauty, fragrant as the kanthal opening on the tall hill east of festive Uranthai.
4.nuance: The man's tying of the bells is the poem's proof of his tenderness: a man who will not wake sleeping pairs of birds is hurrying to his own pair. The rain does the promising before he arrives (கார்செய்தன்றே), as the friend's argument requires.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகளைப் பருவங்காட்டி வற்புறுத்தியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come to the jasmine forest, the season of his promised return

comparisons.tenor: the stag's dark horns, like twisted iron
the drawn reins, taut as strung lute-strings
her beauty, fragrant as the opening kanthal

iraicchi.act: the nectar birds sleep in the flowering boughs together with their mates
iraicchi.sense: the man who will not wake a pair asleep is coming home to rest with his own wife

5.reading: The man tells his heart why he gave up the journey: when he thought of crossing the stony, useless forest where gooseberries fall like dice on the rock and sharp stones cut the toes, she came near unasked, with a faint forced smile, said nothing but stood like a painting as if assenting to the old saying that such leaving is not the way of right, and when, eyes swimming, she sighed over the garland on the head of the son held to her breast, its bright flower lost its colour; seeing that he stayed, for she grieves even with him beside her and would not live if they parted.
5.nuance: Her whole argument is unspoken: she refuses by looking (முன்னம் காட்டி, முகத்தின் உரையா), and the decisive sign is not on her but on the child, the garland withering under her breath. The old maxim she seems to accept, அறத்தாறு அன்று, is the poem's only statement of a rule, and it is attributed to tradition, not to her.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் வயிற் பிரியக் கருதிய தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லிச் செலவழுங்கியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a man weighs crossing the waste for wealth and gives it up

comparisons.tenor: the gooseberries, clear as crystal
the fallen gooseberries on the rock, like gaming dice heaped up
the blunted points of the stones, as if worn down
the ridged sharp stones, set in rows like garden beds
her silence, as if she said 'so be it' to the old saying
her stillness, like a painted figure

6.reading: The wife tells the husband back from a courtesan that yesterday he bathed with his beloved in the Kaveri flood at Uranthai of the generous Thithan, clasping a white reed raft, faces bright like the Poozhiyar's elephant in a pond, his garland crushed on his chest; today he comes and repeats lies about 'the mother of his son, of spotless chastity', mocking her age, which she lets pass: her youth, like Mathi's Kazhar where the otter that fed on vaalai fish among the vallai creepers goes back to rest in the old cane thicket, is long gone, so what can sweet lies do for her.
6.nuance: The otter that feasts in the lotus field and then returns to the old thorny cane is set inside the simile for her lost youth: she pictures him eating among new flowers and sheltering in the old thicket, which is herself. The praise he offers (மாசில் கற்பின், புதல்வன் தாய்) is the true wifely title, and she calls it a lie because it is said to placate her.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையிற் பிரிந்து வந்த தலைமகற்குக் கிழத்தி கூறியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's quarrel with a husband who has been with another woman

comparisons.tenor: the lovers' delighted faces in the water, like the Poozhiyar's elephant in a pond
her youth, rich and gone like Mathi's Kazhar
the husband, who feasts among new women and returns to the old wife

ullurai.tenor: the husband, his courtesan and his aging wife

pairs.situation: he has feasted on a new woman
he has tangled the household's order
he comes back to shelter with the old wife

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the otter of the marutham fields of her own town, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

7.reading: The foster mother, following her daughter who has eloped, recalls her warnings (your breasts have formed, you are no child now, keep away from the old town's spirits and do not go out), and asks a doe with its herd, and a hill girl wearing a tiger-tooth tali who gathers the jackfruit seeds the grazing stag drops, whether they have seen her girl, who fled like a hind that sees a net, with a youth of white spear into this waste, while robbers raiding a cattle-pen have blocked her pursuit.
7.nuance: The first lines quote the very prohibitions the girl escaped; the mother's list of the signs of puberty is also her account of why the girl left. Her questions go to a doe and to a hill girl like her daughter, as if the wild had become the only household left to ask.

colophon.thurai: மகட் போக்கிய செவிலித்தாய் பின் சென்று தான் கானகத்தே கண்டதோர் மகளைக் கண்டு சொல்லியது; நவ்விப் பிணாக்கண்டு சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl has gone with her lover across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the daughter fleeing the house, like a hind that has seen a net

occasion.words: தான் கானகத்தே கண்டதோர் மகளைக் கண்டு சொல்லியது

8.reading: The woman tells her friend, while her lover stands unseen nearby, that even the midnight when the bear clawing termites from the wet anthill makes snakes lose their strength would not be hard to face, if only someone would ask him: in your land, where the tiger drags the boar it killed so the jackfruit slope reeks of flesh and the cow elephant breaks a great tree to ease her mate trapped in a pit, do you who led her off the path even know this road, where she came by lightning flashes without losing her way, gathering her rain-wet hair over her back and wringing it?
8.nuance: She wants the danger she has run spoken to him by someone else; the poem is overheard reproach. The cow elephant crashing down a tree for her mate in the pit is the one tender act among the beasts, and it is what she herself has been doing.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a midnight tryst on the hill slopes

comparisons.tenor: her dark hair, like sapphire

iraicchi.act: the cow elephant breaks a great tree to ease the pain of her mate fallen into a pit
iraicchi.sense: she braves the night for him as the cow labours for her trapped mate, while he does not see what it costs her

9.reading: Returning with his work done, the man tells his heart, the charioteer listening, that it raced ahead of the sleepless chariot past the iruppai-strewn red path and the hill where pestle songs echo with the owl, and asks whether it has already reached her, standing at a corner of the tall house in the evening when calves come home, praying at every chirp of the lizard, and crept up with hand unraised to cover her eyes, touch her braid and stroke her bangled arm.
9.nuance: The man's homecoming is imagined from her side: the evening, the lizard's omen, the game of covering her eyes, all happen in the heart before the body arrives. The road's iruppai and red earth belong to the waste, but the poem's situation is the mullai return and the woman waiting at dusk.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீண்ட தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the work is done and she waits at evening for his return; the waste is only the road

comparisons.tenor: the iruppai buds, like arrow points
the iruppai's red young leaves
the soft hollow iruppai flowers, like butter
the red hill slope, like coral
her braid, like a cow elephant's trunk

10.reading: The friend stops the shore lord leaving after a night meeting and tells him, lord of the coast where birds settle on the old punnai whose buds look like fish eyes, that if he means to part and make the girl's neythal eyes weep he has taken on a hard thing; he must marry her properly and take her, for her beauty is like rich Thondi, where fishermen with new nets share out the horned fish on the sandy shore of the fragrant hamlet.
10.nuance: The friend values the girl in the currency of a Chera port: a public, famous, prosperous town, the opposite of a secret meeting. The fishermen's sharing of the catch is a picture of open, rightful taking, which is what she asks of him (உரிதினின் கொண்டு).

colophon.thurai: இரவுக் குறிவந்து தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்குந் தலைமகனை எதிர்ப்பட்டு நின்று தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai, the fishermen and the lord of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the punnai buds, like fish eyes
her eyes, as neythal flowers
her beauty, rich as Thondi

occasion.words: இரவுக் குறிவந்து தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்குந் தலைமகனை

11.reading: The woman tells her friend that had he taken her with him through the sun-scorched forest where the leafless silk-cotton blooms like rows of festival lamps and the pools have turned to dust, he too would have had her close embrace on the sandbank of the forest stream under the drooping flowered boughs, and her eyes, which now weep every night like dripping flowers as if to fill a dry tank, would have slept.
11.nuance: She turns the usual argument round: the road is not too hard for her; it is the place where their embrace could have been. The colophon reads the poem as her assurance that she will bear up, but what it says is that she does not: the assurance lies in her saying it calmly, not in its content.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்தவிடத்து ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகள் வேறுபாடுகண்டு ஆற்றாளாய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் ஆற்றுவல் என்பதுபடச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-burned forest the man has crossed without her

comparisons.tenor: the sun's disc, red as fire
the silk-cotton in flower, like long rows of festival lamps
the heaped sand of the stream bank, like spread cloth
the embrace, as if body entered body
her streaming eyes, like flowers dripping water
her nightly weeping, as if to fill a dried tank

12.reading: The friend tells the hill lord that the girl's mother loves her more than her own eyes, her father cannot bear her small feet on hard ground, and the two of them are one life like the two-headed bird; on his hill, where an elephant takes the vengai flowers strewn over the hunters' hut for a tiger and flees through the bamboo, if he comes (by night) the gentle girl will not survive.
12.nuance: The household's love is given as the guard itself: the closer they hold her, the less she can slip away. The elephant that bolts from vengai blossom mistaken for a tiger is a hill scene of false alarm; a reader may hear in it the danger of discovery, but it maps to no stated situation. Whether 'we' (யாமே) are the girl and her friend or the girl and her lover is open.

colophon.thurai: "பகற்குறி வாரா நின்ற தலைமகன் தோழியாற் செறிப்பறிவுறுக்கப்பட்டு இரவுக்குறி வாரா வரைவல் என்றாற்கு, அதுவும் மறுத்து வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: millet guards, hill hunters and the vengai of the hill

comparisons.tenor: the two women (or the two lovers), one life like the two-headed bird

occasion.words: இரவுக்குறி வாரா வரைவல் என்றாற்கு, அதுவும் மறுத்து வரைவு கடாயது

13.reading: The friend tells the man that even if the wealth he would earn were as great as the fruitful sacrifice of the Pandya's warrior, lord of Kodai, who wears the pearl of his sea and the sandal of his hill and gives to suppliants without limit except the short while it takes to teach a pit-caught elephant to obey, he should not leave his gentle companion in these days of cold dew, when the lonely north wind sways the forked paddy in the wide fields and makes the white heron on the sugarcane cry; let the wealth go, and the nights in a clean bed without embrace.
13.nuance: The patron's limitless giving is the measure, and the friend uses it to set a ceiling: no wealth, not even such a man's, is worth a winter apart. The two clauses of wishing (நோய் இன்றாக செய்பொருள்; கவவுஇன் புறாமைக் கழிக) can be read as bitter dismissal or as a blessing on his going, which is why the colophon allows that she consented.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் வயிற் பிரியலுற்ற தலைமகனைத் தோழி செலவழங்கு வித்தது; உடம்பட்டதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend argues against a departure for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the wealth he would earn, measured against the patron's great sacrifice
the paddy's young blades, like flame tips

14.reading: The bard tells his companions that the wife said to him, 'if he does not remember us even in this evening, when the stag nuzzles its doe and leaps grazing on the red-earth road strewn with kaya flowers, herders deck themselves in the jasmine land and good cows, udders dripping, low for their calves as they crowd into the common, what will become of us by morning, bard?'; unable to answer, he played his lute, praised the god, steadied his grief and went toward the husband, and now he has seen his tall chariot coming, wheels roaring like thunder-clouds.
14.nuance: The bard's own answer to her question is not words but music and prayer, and then a sighting; the poem moves from her evening to his seeing. Evening in the jasmine land is the hour when everything returns to its pair, which is why it is the measure of his forgetting.

colophon.thurai: பாணன் தனக்குப் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: evening in the jasmine land, the herders and cows coming home

comparisons.tenor: the red earth of the road, like lac
the hills, like coral studded with gems
the roar of the chariot wheels, like thunder of rain clouds

iraicchi.act: the stag holds its young doe close and leaps as it grazes beside her
iraicchi.sense: in this season even the stag keeps to its mate, yet the husband has not come home to his

15.reading: The mother whose daughter has eloped wishes that, if her fierce longing can be granted, the old town of the man's many hamlets may know how to welcome her, as the Kosar's Thulu country, with its peacock groves, shelters empty-handed travellers; for her soft-shouldered dear one, leaving her friends and mother lonely, has slipped the strict guard of a house like Nannan's fortress Pazhi and gone with him on the road where bears scatter the iruppai flowers and konrai pods, set on her sweet companion.
15.nuance: Her grief turns into a blessing on the stranger's town. The house is likened to Nannan's guarded Pazhi so that the breach looks like the fall of a fort; the girl's resolve (இன்துணைப் படர்ந்த கொள்கை) is acknowledged, not condemned.

colophon.thurai: மகட் போக்கிய தாய் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has gone with her lover across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the man's old town, hoped to be as hospitable as the Kosar's Thulu country
the guarded house, like Nannan's fortress Pazhi
her shoulders, rounded like hill bamboo

16.reading: The wife tells her husband, who claims he knows no other woman, that she saw a sharp-toothed girl find their little son alone in the chariot street, lift him to her ornamented breast crying 'come, my life!' when no one was looking; she went up and asked 'why so flustered, spotless girl? are you his mother too?', embraced her, and watched her bow her head, scratch the ground and stand ashamed like one caught in a secret; and so, she asks, did she not treat her kindly, since that goddess-like woman is fit to be his son's mother?
16.nuance: The proof against his denial is the courtesan's love for the child, and the wife's weapon is courtesy: she embraces the rival and then, with full irony, ranks her as fit to be the son's mother, which is the title the husband had denied anyone else could claim.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையர் சேரியினின்றும் வந்த தலைமகன் யாரையும் அறியேனென்றாற்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's quarrel over a rival, with the son between them

comparisons.tenor: the child's spotless palm, like a lotus petal
the child's mouth, like coral-red gem
the courtesan's shame, like one who has owned to a theft
the courtesan, like an unapproachable goddess of the sky

17.reading: The foster mother remembers that her girl, if she threw a ball a little or played jacks with her friends, would say 'mother, I am tired' and lie in her arms with sweat on her brow; now, forgetting kin and nurse, she has crossed her proud father's strict guard and given her whole heart to a stranger, and the nurse asks whether those little anklet feet can walk the waterless waste where salt-carters' calls echo in the hills and the falling silk-cotton flowers flicker like festival lamps or like stars at dawn, under the dark hill that bars the way.
17.nuance: The whole poem rests on one contrast: a girl too tired for a ball game now walking the waste. The silk-cotton flowers like lamps in an old town's festival bring the home town into the wilderness, the place she has left as a light falling on her road.

colophon.thurai: மகட் போக்கிய செவிலித்தாய் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has left her father's guard for a stranger

comparisons.tenor: the salt caravan's march, like a whole town on the move
the falling silk-cotton flowers, like the flickering lamps of a festival
the scattered flowers, like the stars at dawn

18.reading: The friend asks the hill lord whether anyone comes here at midnight, crossing like a fierce boar the dreadful ford of the forest torrent, its water hidden under fallen flowers, where crocodiles sleep in the eddies and the flood drags off a wild elephant; if her friend suffers harm even for a day she will not live after, and even on safe paths those who go often slip, so they live in fear; let him come by day and meet her in the kanthal grove below the honey-combed hill of their garden, and hold the soft shoulders, like bamboo, that her mother reared.
18.nuance: She does not forbid the meeting; she moves it. The danger she names is the road's, but the argument is also about discovery: the frequent traveller slips (பயில வழங்குநர் ... இழுக்குவர்), and a secret repeated becomes known.

colophon.thurai: தோழி இரவு வருவானைப் பகல் வர வென்றது.

thinai_evidence.note: a midnight tryst in the hills

comparisons.tenor: the lover fording the flood, unafraid like a fierce boar
her shoulders, like the bamboo between its nodes

19.reading: The man, on his way for wealth, tells his heart that it neither stayed with her then nor will cross the hills with him now, where the kite cries wearily from the tall yaa and the owl hoots like a drum; if it means to stay behind, let it go back, prosper, and not forget him, once it has embraced the tired drooping back of his love, who sits unmoving with a lamp for company, her dark lily eyelids gone red and burning with every thought of him, hot tears falling, bangles slipping from her wrist, wilting like a creeper that has shed its flowers.
19.nuance: Here the heart that stands behind (பின்நின்று) holds back toward her, where in Akananuru 3 the heart behind drives him on; the man splits from his heart and sends it home in his stead. The lamp as her only companion is the poem's centre.

colophon.thurai: நெஞ்சினாற் பொருள் வலிக்கப்பட்டுப் பிரிந்த தலைமகன்

thinai_evidence.note: a man gone for wealth parts from his own heart on the waste road

comparisons.tenor: the owl's harsh call, like the throb of a drum
her eyelids gone red with weeping, like nara petals
her eyelids, once like dark kuvalai petals
her wasting body, like a creeper that has shed its flowers
the lamp, her only companion

20.reading: The friend tells the girl, while the lover stands unseen nearby, that their days of chasing birds from her father's drying fish, resting in the punnai's shade, digging out red crabs, swinging on the thazhai-root swing, playing with the waves and coming home in leaf skirts are over: mother, taking the word of the town's spiteful women, has put her under guard, because there is a chariot with fine horses that circles the moonlit sand of the great ford regardless of day or night.
20.nuance: The list of shore games is a portrait of a girlhood now closed by gossip, and it is spoken for the hidden lover to hear: the last line names his chariot as the cause, so the report is also a summons to marry.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்த தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai, screw pine and crabs of the backwater shore

comparisons.tenor: the town's gossip, a possessing spirit that has seized the town

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon breaks off after தோழி; the poem's addressee is the girl (தோழி, line 13)

links.note: Both invocations, ascribed to Perundevanar, list Shiva by the same marks: the konrai garland and chaplet, the bull, the dark throat, the crescent, the matted hair. Akananuru 0 says Umai is joined to him (சேர்ந்தோள் உமையே); Purananuru 1 says the woman's form is one part of him that he can hide within himself.
links.teaches: Placed side by side, the two openings show each anthology choosing the god's form that suits its matter: the love anthology gives him a consort beside him, the outer anthology a body that holds the woman within it and shelters all lives.

links.note: Both are Mamoolanar's paalai poems that use Avi's Pothini: in 1 the woman fears the man has forgotten a vow fixed like Pothini's lac-set stone; in 61 the friend tells her he cannot stay away, forgetting her breast, as fine as Pothini.
links.teaches: One poet hands the same town to both sides of the separation, so Pothini is the woman's measure of the promise in one poem and the friend's measure of the man's longing in the other: the fear and its answer are built from one image.

links.note: Both speak in the woman's voice after a promise not to part is broken by his leaving: the Kural asks if the believer is at fault; Akananuru 1 asks whether he has forgotten (மறந்தனர் கொல்லோ).
links.teaches: The Kural turns the broken promise into a question of blame, while the Sangam heroine keeps it a question of memory; the poem shows a woman who will not yet say he broke his word, which the couplet's moral question has already assumed.

links.note: Both are Kapilar's poems in which the friend presses the hill lord to marry: in 2 she still allows that he may come at night past the watchmen, under the vengai and the moon; in 12 she refuses night meetings outright and says the girl will not live if he comes.
links.teaches: Read in sequence they show the friend's pressure tightening from an ironic permission to a flat refusal, so the varaivu demand is a process with stages, not a single plea.

links.note: Both men speak to the heart that stands behind them (பின்நின்று): in 3 it drives him from behind toward wealth (பின்நின்று துரக்கும்), in 19 it plans to stay behind with her (பின்நின்று ஒழியச் சூழ்ந்தனை).
links.teaches: The heart at the man's back is a fixed paalai figure that can push either way, toward the road or toward home, so in these poems the heart is not one side of the debate but the place where the debate happens.

links.note: Both place a spot by the formula 'east of Uranthai' (உறந்தைக் குணாது): in Akananuru 4 the tall hill whose kanthal she smells of, in Purananuru 395 Pidavur, the patron Sathan's town.
links.teaches: The same coordinates serve a patron's address and a woman's fragrance, which shows that akam's landscape was drawn on the real map of Chola country that puram poets used for their patrons.

links.note: Both answer a man's announced departure for wealth: in Kural 1151 she says 'if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive'; in Akananuru 5 she says nothing, and he gives up the journey.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the refusal its sharpest words, and the Sangam poem shows the same refusal working without any: from the man's side, it is the unspoken sign and the withering garland on the child that stop him.

links.note: Both Paranar poems throw at the husband the same scandal, bathing with his beloved in the Kaveri flood (நீ வெய்யோளொடு), and both set it in Chola names: Thithan's Uranthai and Mathi's Kazhar. In 6 the wife speaks; in 226 the friend refuses him entry.
links.teaches: The repeated phrase and place-names show one marutham scandal reused by its poet from two speakers, so the bath in the Kaveri was a known situation that a hearer recognised from a few words.

links.note: Both use the formula of Thithan the great giver (மாவண் தித்தன்) and his paddy-rich Uranthai: Purananuru 352 likens the fine gifts offered for a girl, and refused, to Uranthai; Akananuru 6 sets the husband's riverside affair at Uranthai.
links.teaches: A single praise formula for a Chola chief served the puram poet as the measure of a refused bride-price and the akam poet as the stage of a husband's betrayal, which shows how much shared fame the two kinds of poem drew on.

links.note: Both are Kayamanar's poems of the foster mother after the girl's elopement: in 17 she sits at home picturing the girl's small feet on the waste; in 7 she has followed into the forest and is asking a doe and a hill girl for news.
links.teaches: Together they give the foster mother's grief two stages, imagination at home and pursuit on the road, and show that the poet built the udanpokku mother as a figure who moves through the story.

links.note: Both speak in the voice of the man returning from work to an evening at home: Kural 1268 wishes the king's war won so that he may feast with his wife at evening; Akananuru 9's work is done and his heart has gone ahead to her at the evening when calves come home.
links.teaches: The Kural names the evening the man looks forward to, and the Sangam poem fills it from the woman's side, her prayer at the lizard's chirp and the game of covered eyes, with his heart arriving before his chariot.

links.note: Both make the Chera port Thondi famous for its shore and its fragrance: Purananuru 48's bard calls it his own town, smelling of neythal, to direct another bard to its king; Akananuru 10's friend likens the girl's beauty to rich Thondi.
links.teaches: The friend values a girl in the terms a bard used for a king's town, so a woman's worth in akam could be stated in the public currency of puram praise, as a reason for open marriage rather than secret meeting.

links.note: Both praise the lord of Kodai (கோடைப் பொருநன் / கோடைப் பொருந) for giving elephants: Purananuru 205 says the bard's troupe never leaves him without elephants and chariots; Akananuru 13 says he gives to suppliants without limit, pausing only to tame a pit-caught elephant.
links.teaches: The friend in Akananuru 13 takes the very generosity that Purananuru 205 praises and makes it a ceiling: even wealth that large is not worth a winter apart, so puram praise becomes an akam argument against seeking wealth.

links.note: Both are mothers after an elopement: the mother in 15 ends by wishing hospitality on the man's town and acknowledging her daughter's resolve; the foster mother in 17 cannot get past the girl's small, tired feet.
links.teaches: Set together, the two mothers show that the udanpokku lament could close in blessing or in fear, and that the birth mother is the one given the larger acceptance of the daughter's choice.

links.note: Both are Kapilar's friend speaking to the hill lord about his night visits: in 18 she asks him to come by day instead, to the kanthal grove; in 12, by its colophon after day meetings have been stopped, she refuses the night as well and demands marriage.
links.teaches: The two poems show the friend's options closing one by one, night refused for day and then day lost to confinement, so the only path left is marriage, the end both poems are built toward.

links.note: Both join the town's gossip (கவ்வை, கௌவை) and the mother's response: Kural 1147 says gossip is manure and the mother's words water to the woman's sickness; in Akananuru 20 the mother acts on the gossip and puts the girl under guard.
links.teaches: The Kural reads gossip and the mother as feeding love from within, while the Sangam poem shows their outward effect, confinement, and uses it to press the hidden lover to marry, so the couplet's paradox has a practical role in the akam plot.
